# Important System Calls {#appendix-c-important-system-calls}

These are some of the more important system calls to use when dealing
with Linux.`#index("System calls")`{=typst} For most cases, however, it is best to use library functions
rather than direct system calls, because the system calls were designed
to be minimalistic while the library functions were designed to be easy
to program with. Most programs on Linux, whatever the language they are
written in, reach the system calls through the
[GNU C Library][AC-GNU-C] or through the standard library of their
language.

To make a system call on x86-64 Linux:

-   Put the system call number in _%rax_.

-   Put the parameters, in order, in _%rdi_, _%rsi_, _%rdx_, _%r10_,
    _%r8_ and _%r9_. No system call takes more than six.

-   Run the `syscall` instruction.

-   The result comes back in _%rax_. A value between -4095 and -1 means
    an error: it is the negative of the error number (for example, -2
    is `ENOENT`, \"no such file or directory\").

The `syscall` instruction overwrites _%rcx_ and _%r11_. All of the
other registers, except _%rax_, keep their values.

Table C-1. Important Linux System Calls.

**System Call**: _%rax_.

---

**read**: _0_.

> - **%rdi**: File descriptor.
  - **%rsi**: Buffer start.
  - **%rdx**: Buffer size.
  - Reads into the given buffer. Returns the number of bytes read, 0
    at the end of the file, or an error number.

**write**: _1_.

> - **%rdi**: File descriptor.
  - **%rsi**: Buffer start.
  - **%rdx**: Buffer size.
  - Writes the buffer to the file descriptor. Returns the number of
    bytes written or an error number.

**close**: _3_.

> - **%rdi**: File descriptor.
  - Closes the given file descriptor.

**lseek**: _8_.

> - **%rdi**: File descriptor.
  - **%rsi**: Offset.
  - **%rdx**: Mode.
  - Repositions where you are in the given file. The mode (called the
    "whence") should be 0 for absolute positioning, 1 for relative
    positioning and 2 for positioning relative to the end of the file.

**mmap**: _9_.

> - **%rdi**: Suggested address (usually 0, to let the kernel choose).
  - **%rsi**: Length in bytes.
  - **%rdx**: Protection (for example 3 for reading and writing).
  - **%r10**: Flags (for example 0x22 for private memory not backed
    by a file).
  - **%r8**: File descriptor (-1 if there is no file).
  - **%r9**: Offset in the file.
  - Maps a region of memory into the program and returns its address.

**brk**: _12_.

> - **%rdi**: New system break.
  - Sets the system break, i.e. the end of the data section of the
    program. Returns the new system break. If the parameter is 0, it
    simply returns the current system break.

**ioctl**: _16_.

> - **%rdi**: File descriptor.
  - **%rsi**: Request.
  - **%rdx**: Arguments.
  - This is used to set parameters on device files. Its actual usage
    varies based on the type of file or device your descriptor references.

**pipe**: _22_.

> - **%rdi**: Pipe array.
  - Creates two file descriptors, where writing on one produces data to
    read on the other. _%rdi_ is a pointer to two longs (four bytes
    each) of storage to hold the file descriptors.

**dup**: _32_.

> - **%rdi**: File descriptor.
  - Returns a new file descriptor that works just like the existing file
    descriptor.

**getpid**: _39_.

> - Returns the process ID of the current process.

**exit**: _60_.

> - **%rdi**: Return value. Only the lowest byte (0 to 255) reaches
    the shell.
  - Exits the program. (A program with several threads uses
    **exit_group**, number 231, to end all of them.)

**chdir**: _80_.

> - **%rdi**: Null-terminated directory name.
  - Changes the current directory of your program.

**mkdir**: _83_.

> - **%rdi**: Null-terminated directory name.
  - **%rsi**: Permission mode.
  - Creates the given directory. Assumes all directories leading up to it
    already exist.

**rmdir**: _84_.

> - **%rdi**: Null-terminated directory name.
  - Removes the given directory.

**openat**: _257_.

> - **%rdi**: Directory file descriptor. -100 (`AT_FDCWD`) means the
    current directory.
  - **%rsi**: Null-terminated file name.
  - **%rdx**: Option list.
  - **%r10**: Permission mode.
  - Opens the given file. Returns the file descriptor or an error
    number. If the file name starts with `/`, the directory is ignored.
    The older system call **open** (number 2) does the same without the
    directory parameter; current libraries use `openat`.

---

The complete list of system calls for x86-64, with their numbers, is in
the Linux source code, in the file
[arch/x86/entry/syscalls/syscall_64.tbl][AC-Syscall-table]. On your own
computer, the numbers are in `/usr/include/asm/unistd_64.h`. The
[syscall.sh][AC-Call-convention] web site shows the numbers and the
registers for each architecture. You can also get more information about
a system call by typing in `man 2 openat` (or the name of another
system call), which will return you the information about the system
call from section 2 of the UNIX manual. The manual describes the library
function with the same name, but its parameters are the same as the
system call\'s, in the same order. `man 2 syscall` lists the registers
used to make system calls on each architecture.

[AC-Call-convention]: https://syscall.sh/
